title: Whether science changes by revolutions is contested
body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry "Scientific Revolutions" surveys a dispute about how science changes. One account, associated with Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, says that normal research inside a shared framework is sometimes replaced wholesale when anomalies accumulate and a new framework takes over. Other historians and philosophers argue that the change is more continuous, that old and new practices overlap, and that the word revolution imports a political metaphor the record does not always fit. The label "the Scientific Revolution" for Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries is part of the same argument. It is a name for a cluster of changes in astronomy, mechanics, and method. It is not a date on which science began. This card does not decide the dispute. It marks the label as contested.
said_by: Historiographical dispute surveyed by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

contested_views.position: Science sometimes changes by revolutionary replacement of a framework, not only by accumulation.
contested_views.held_by: Thomas Kuhn, as surveyed in the Stanford Encyclopedia entry

contested_views.position: The changes are more continuous, and revolution is a misleading metaphor.
contested_views.held_by: Critics of Kuhn surveyed in the same entry
